paper_context.research_question: Can an attention-based neural sequence-to-sequence model be trained to map natural-language utterances directly to executable SQL, and can an online feedback loop with lightweight user feedback plus selective crowd annotation rapidly bootstrap and improve such a semantic parser for new domains?
main_claims: A neural sequence-to-sequence model with attention can directly generate full SQL queries from natural language with accuracy comparable to prior semantic-parsing approaches that target logical forms.
Schema-agnostic synthetic schema templates plus paraphrase-based data augmentation provide a practical way to bootstrap models for new domains without manual, database-specific engineering.

An online interactive learning loop that solicits simple binary (and slightly finer-grained) user feedback and selectively sends incorrect examples to crowd workers for SQL annotations enables rapid domain adaptation from scratch and reduces annotation effort over time.
Entity anonymization via TF-IDF search and post-processing lets the model generalize across entity mentions and fill concrete values in generated SQL.
The approach is practical: a small online deployment for an academic paper database yielded steady improvement across three stages and produced a released SCHOLAR dataset of utterance–SQL pairs.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Denotation (execution) accuracy of generated SQL on benchmark datasets (Geo880, ATIS) compared to prior work
Ablation studies measuring contributions of schema templates and paraphrase augmentation
Effectiveness of interactive learning: accuracy improvement across deployment stages and reduction in annotation effort (fraction of queries requiring crowd labeling)
Quality and noise characteristics of user feedback (false positives/negatives) and robustness of learning to such noisy feedback
Practicality metrics: initial bootstrapping performance with synthetic templates, required amount of human annotation, and deployability to a real domain (SCHOLAR) including user study outcomes
Generality of approach across schemas (schema-agnostic template applicability) and handling of entity identification via anonymization

argument_focus: Feasibility of mapping natural language directly to full SQL using attention-based seq2seq models.
Practical bootstrapping of new-domain parsers via schema-agnostic templates and paraphrase augmentation.
Efficacy of an interactive feedback loop combining lightweight user signals and selective crowd annotation to reduce labeling effort.
Entity anonymization and reconstruction pipeline as crucial engineering for generalization.
contribution_targets: A neural seq2seq model architecture and training regime for direct natural-language-to-SQL generation (Section 4.1).
A data-augmentation method combining schema-agnostic templates and PPDB paraphrasing to bootstrap models (Section 4.3).
An interactive training algorithm (Algorithm 1) that incorporates user feedback and crowd labeling for iterative improvement (Section 3).
An operational anonymization and entity resolution procedure using TF-IDF for entity matching (Section 4.2).
A released SCHOLAR utterance–SQL dataset and demonstration of a small-scale live deployment (Section 6.3, 6.2).
evaluation_targets: Denotation (execution) accuracy of generated SQL on GEO880, ATIS, and SCHOLAR compared to prior methods (Section 5, 6.3).
Ablation effects of schema templates and paraphrase augmentation on model performance (Section 5.3; Section 6.4).
Interactive learning curves: accuracy improvement and fraction of queries requiring crowd annotation across stages/batch sizes (Section 6.2; Section 6.4 Table 7).
Quality and error rates of user feedback (false positives/negatives) and resulting impact on training data quality (Section 6.2 Table 6).
Entity linking performance (precision/recall) of the TF-IDF anonymization approach and its effect on final SQL correctness (Section 4.2).
Robustness of model to noisy paraphrase augmentation and noisy crowd annotations (implicit across Sections 4.3 and 6.2).
uncertainty_flags: Comparability: Prior works report heterogeneous metrics (logical form vs denotation) and sometimes use different splits (Geo700 vs Geo880); exact comparability of reported 'comparable performance' is uncertain.
Scale/generalization: Online experiment is small (30 users across 3 stages); external validity to larger, diverse user populations and more complex schemas is uncertain.
Annotation quality: Crowd annotation process, worker selection, inter-annotator agreement, and SQL labeling costs are not fully detailed; label noise impact is uncertain.
Entity linking: TF-IDF entity resolution effectiveness is not quantified; failure modes and coverage limits are unclear.
Paraphrase noise: Random single-word PPDB replacements could introduce semantic drift; magnitude of beneficial vs harmful paraphrases is not fully quantified.
Simulation realism: Simulated interactive experiments assume perfect feedback; real-world feedback is noisy as shown elsewhere, so simulated gains may overestimate real gains.
chaining_notes: Downstream reviewers should test the pipeline end-to-end because several components (entity anonymization, paraphrase augmentation, seq2seq decoding, and feedback-driven relabeling) interact nonlinearly: e.g., entity-link failures can cause user feedback noise which triggers crowd labeling and affects retraining.

Specific empirical checks useful for later stages: (a) reproduce benchmark denotation accuracies and compare using identical preprocessing/splits to prior works; (b) measure entity linking precision/recall on held-out utterances; (c) quantify gain from templates vs paraphrasing separately with confidence intervals; (d) measure effect of user feedback noise by injecting controlled label noise into simulated interactive runs; (e) analyze crowd annotation quality (agreement, error types) and cost per example.
When testing interactive claims, vary batch sizes, user populations, and template coverage to assess robustness and operational trade-offs (annotation frequency vs. model improvement).

Track provenance of training examples added via user-corrected vs crowd-annotated labels to detect whether noisy user-accepted incorrect predictions (false positives) accumulate and degrade performance over time.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that (1) an attention-based seq2seq model can directly generate executable SQL from natural language with performance comparable to prior semantic-parsing systems, (2) schema-agnostic synthetic templates plus PPDB paraphrase augmentation can bootstrap new-domain models without database-specific engineering, and (3) an online interactive loop using lightweight user feedback plus selective crowd annotation enables rapid domain adaptation while reducing annotation effort. Key engineering pieces (entity anonymization via TF-IDF, anonymized token filling, beam decoding) glue the pipeline together. Evidence includes denotation-based benchmark evaluations (Geo880, ATIS), ablations showing paraphrasing benefits, simulated interactive experiments (perfect feedback), and a small live 3-stage deployment producing the SCHOLAR dataset. The argument chain is coherent in high-level structure, but several links are weak or under-specified: comparability claims conflate denotation and logical-form metrics and do not control for preprocessing/splits; template generality and template/manual design effort are under-quantified; entity linking effectiveness is asserted qualitatively without measured precision/recall; and the online experiment is small-scale with noisy user feedback whose long-term effects are not explored. Overall, the reasoning is plausible and supported by empirical tests, but its external validity and some component-level claims need further empirical substantiation and clearer qualification.
logical_argument_graph: Node A: Practical problem — building NL interfaces to databases for new domains is hard due to feature engineering / limited expressivity of prior logical-form approaches.
Node B: Solution proposal — adapt attention-based neural seq2seq models to map utterances directly to SQL (no intermediate representation).
Edge A->B: Motivates direct SQL mapping to leverage SQL expressivity and easier crowd annotation (SQL is widely understood).
Node C: Bootstrapping data — use schema-agnostic SQL templates instantiated from schema graph + PPDB paraphrase augmentation to create initial training data.
Edge B->C: Model needs initial data; templates + paraphrasing supply synthetic examples enabling cold-start.
Node D: Entity handling — anonymize entities using TF-IDF over DB entities and reconstruct values post-generation.
Edge B->D: Entity anonymization reduces sparsity and allows the model to learn schema-level patterns.

Node E: Interactive loop — deploy model, collect user feedback (5-way), accept 'correct'/'incomplete' into training, send incorrect ones to crowd for SQL annotation; retrain iteratively (Algorithm 1).
Edge C+D->E: Template seed and entity pipeline enable useful initial responses to elicit user feedback.

Node F: Empirical evidence — (i) Denotation accuracy on GEO880/ATIS comparable to prior work; (ii) Ablations show paraphrasing helps; (iii) Simulated interactive experiments indicate learning curves and reduced annotation with batching; (iv) Small live deployment (3 stages, 30 users) yields 63.5% correct after stage 3 and produced SCHOLAR dataset.
Edge E->F: Interactive pipeline produces labeled examples and shows decreasing annotation fraction over stages.
Node G: Claims about practicality and portability — approach generalizes across schemas, can port to other query languages, and is deployable in realistic settings.
Edge F->G: Empirical and deployment evidence are used to support practicality claim.

Weak links flagged: comparability of benchmark numbers (denotation vs LF); template manual effort vs 'no manual engineering' claim; lack of measured entity-link accuracy; small scale/noisy live deployment threatens external validity.

concerns.title: Comparability of benchmark results
concerns.description: The claim of 'comparable performance' mixes denotation-based accuracy and logical-form metrics across prior work and does not control for dataset preprocessing/split differences or report statistical significance.
evidence: Section 5.3 compares denotation accuracies to prior works that sometimes report logical-form accuracy or use Geo700 vs Geo880; shared analysis notes heterogenous metrics.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Recompute baselines under identical preprocessing/splits and report paired significance tests or confidence intervals; explicitly report which prior works use denotation vs LF and, if possible, run oracle/equivalence checks.

concerns.title: Under-specified entity linking evaluation
concerns.description: TF-IDF based entity anonymization is central to pipeline, but no quantitative evaluation of its entity linking precision/recall or downstream impact on SQL correctness is provided.
evidence: Section 4.2 describes TF-IDF matching qualitatively; shared analysis flags absence of precision/recall measurements.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a held-out annotation set for entity mentions, report entity linking precision/recall/F1 and an ablation showing model performance with perfect vs. TF-IDF linking to quantify impact.

concerns.title: Template manual effort overstated
concerns.description: Claim that bootstrapping requires 'no database-specific engineering' is inconsistent with the fact that 22 manually designed templates were created; template creation cost and coverage are not quantified.
evidence: Section 4.3: authors define 22 language/SQL templates; Section 6.4 notes templates did not help ATIS because query patterns differ.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the manual effort required to produce templates, report time/effort to create them, and provide analysis of coverage (what fraction of user intents/templates match). Consider automating template generation or clearly qualify the claim.

concerns.title: Limited scale and realism of live interactive experiment
concerns.description: The online deployment had only 30 users over three stages; simulated experiments assume perfect feedback. This raises concern about external validity and long-term behavior under noisy feedback.
evidence: Section 6.2: three stages, 10 users per stage; Section 6.4: simulation assumes perfect feedback; user feedback error rates reported only for final stage.
Shared analysis notes small-scale experiment and potential harmful accumulation of false-positive user feedback.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report more granular timelines, per-user statistics, and ablations where controlled noise is injected in simulations to match observed feedback error rates; if possible, run a larger or longer deployment or provide bootstrapped simulation matched to observed noise.

concerns.title: Paraphrase noise not quantified
concerns.description: PPDB-based random single-word substitution is used widely, but the paper does not quantify how often paraphrases change meaning or introduce ungrammatical inputs and how that affects learning.
evidence: Section 4.3 describes random non-stopword replacement; Section 5.3 claims paraphrasing helps but lacks detailed stats on harmful paraphrases.
Shared analysis flags potential semantic drift.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report the distribution and magnitude of paraphrase impacts (e.g., human or automatic semantic-similarity checks), include ablation with filtered/high-precision PPDB subsets, and measure variance in results.

concerns.title: Potential harm from false-positive user feedback
concerns.description: Although reported user false-positive rate is low (6.3%), incorrect 'correct' markings add wrong labeled examples to training and could degrade the model if not controlled; the long-term dynamics of such errors are not analyzed.
evidence: Section 6.2 reports 6.3% of incorrect queries were deemed correct by users; algorithm adds 'correct' examples to training set.
Shared analysis notes asymmetry of harm.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Implement and evaluate safeguards (e.g., conservatively accepting 'correct' only when paired with high model confidence, or using redundancy/crowd-checks for borderline cases) and run simulations that model accumulation of false-positive labels.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes an applied system: an attention-based seq2seq model (bidirectional LSTM encoder, global attention, LSTM decoder, beam search) that directly generates SQL from natural language. To enable rapid bootstrapping in new domains, authors use 22 manually authored schema-agnostic SQL/language templates and paraphrase augmentation via PPDB; entities are anonymized via TF-IDF lookup to map spans to database entities. An interactive loop collects granular user feedback (5 options); examples marked incorrect are selectively sent to crowd workers for SQL annotation and then used to retrain the model. Empirical evidence includes batch benchmark results (denotation accuracy on GEO880 and ATIS, with ablations), simulated interactive runs (perfect feedback), and a small live three-stage deployment on an academic database producing the SCHOLAR dataset (816 examples). The primary claims are that seq2seq can match prior semantic-parsing performance when outputting SQL, templates+paraphrasing bootstrap new domains, the online feedback+crowd loop reduces annotation effort and improves accuracy, and that TF-IDF anonymization suffices for entity handling. Key methodological dependencies include comparability of denotation metrics, quality and scale of user feedback and crowd labels, template coverage, paraphrase noise, and entity-linking accuracy. Several components interact nonlinearly (entity linking -> execution -> user feedback -> annotation decisions), so end-to-end reproducibility and robustness checks are essential but partially missing.
logical_argument_graph: If an encoder-decoder with attention can learn mappings from anonymized utterances to anonymized SQL tokens (trained with augmented examples), then it can generate correct SQL denotations on benchmarks (C1).

If schema-agnostic SQL templates instantiated via schema graph joins plus paraphrases cover a useful fraction of user queries, then they can bootstrap an initial model and motivate early user interaction (C2).

If users can reliably flag correct vs incorrect executed results and crowd workers can supply correct SQL for flagged errors, adding these labeled examples to training will improve accuracy and reduce future annotation needs (C3).
If TF-IDF retrieval over database entity names accurately maps spans to entity types, anonymization preserves semantics and later re-insertion of concrete values yields correct executions (C4).

Empirical evidence: batch denotation accuracies on GEO880/ATIS near prior methods; ablations indicate paraphrasing helps; simulated interactive learning with perfect feedback shows reduced annotation fraction; a small live deployment shows staged accuracy improvements and produced SCHOLAR.

identified_claims.claim_text: An attention-based neural sequence-to-sequence model can be trained to directly generate full SQL queries from natural-language utterances, achieving denotation (execution) accuracy on GEO880 and ATIS that is comparable to prior semantic-parsing approaches that target logical forms.

Exact numeric test details (standard errors, statistical tests, precise preprocessing) are not fully reproduced; denotation matches can mask semantically different queries.

identified_claims.claim_text: Schema-agnostic synthetic schema templates combined with paraphrase augmentation provide a practical way to bootstrap models for new domains without manual, database-specific engineering.

Simulations show templates help early batches for GEO880 but not ATIS.

Effectiveness varies by domain (helpful for GEO880 early stages, not for ATIS); template coverage relative to real-world query distribution is not quantified.

identified_claims.claim_text: An online interactive learning loop that solicits simple binary (and slightly finer-grained) user feedback and selectively sends incorrect examples to crowd workers for SQL annotations enables rapid domain adaptation from scratch and reduces annotation effort over time.

Live three-stage experiment increased correct fraction from 25% to 63.51% after two rounds of retraining and reduced annotation fraction per stage; simulated experiments show reduced annotation with smaller batch sizes (Table 7).

User feedback is noisy (6.1% false negatives, 6.3% false positives in final stage); long-term accumulation of false positives (incorrect accepted SQL) is not analyzed.

identified_claims.claim_text: Entity anonymization using TF-IDF search over database entities and incremental type placeholders permits flexible entity matching and allows models to generalize and fill concrete values in generated SQL.

Qualitative examples (Donald Knuth vs Donald E. Knuth) mentioned.

TF-IDF may fail on paraphrases, pronouns, or ambiguous/novel mentions; error propagation into the interactive loop is not measured.

identified_claims.claim_text: Using PPDB-based paraphrase augmentation consistently improves model performance during training and interactive learning.
evidence: Ablation statements: paraphrasing 'consistently helps'; Figures and experiments indicate paraphrasing boosts early and ongoing performance.
Paraphrase method: random non-stopword replacement using PPDB large one-one and one-many paraphrases.
uncertainty_flags: Exact numeric effect sizes, variance, and statistical significance of paraphrasing are not fully reported in-text; potential for semantic drift from random substitutions is not analyzed.

identified_claims.claim_text: A small online deployment for an academic paper database learned a semantic parser from scratch over three days, produced steady improvement across stages, and yielded a released SCHOLAR dataset (816 utterance–SQL pairs) with a parser reaching 67% accuracy in supervised setting.
evidence: Three-stage live experiment with 10 users per stage produced 63.51% correct in final stage; authors release SCHOLAR train/test split and report 67% supervised accuracy.
Dataset creation pipeline included crowd-annotated additional utterances (not used in live loop).
uncertainty_flags: Live deployment scale (30 users) and duration (3 stages) are small; representativeness of user queries is unknown.
SCHOLAR includes crowd-labeled examples outside the live process; provenance, inter-annotator agreement, and noise are not deeply characterized.

identified_claims.claim_text: User-provided feedback, using five granular options, has low enough error rates (6.1% false negatives, 6.3% false positives) to allow the interactive learning pipeline to improve models despite noisy signals.
evidence: Reported error rates from final live stage analysis: 6.1% correct SQL marked wrong, 6.3% incorrect SQL marked correct.
Authors claim this is low enough for models to improve.
uncertainty_flags: Error rates are reported for the final stage only and may not generalize across user populations, domains, or query complexity.
Asymmetric harm of false positives (accepting incorrect SQL) is not quantified with respect to model degradation over iterations.

concerns.title: Comparability and metric mismatch with prior work
concerns.description: The paper compares denotation accuracy of SQL outputs to prior works that often report logical-form exact match or use different dataset splits; without standardized preprocessing, splits, and uncertainty estimates the claim of 'comparable performance' is not fully supported.

concerns.description: TF-IDF-based entity anonymization is central to system correctness, but there is no reported precision/recall, failure modes, or effect of entity linking errors on SQL correctness.

concerns.title: Paraphrase augmentation plausibility and noise analysis missing

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include controlled experiments measuring effect size of paraphrasing (with CI), manual inspection of a random sample of paraphrases for semantic fidelity, and compare extreme PPDB size variants (small vs large) or rule-based constrained paraphrasing.

concerns.title: Simulated interactive experiments use optimistic feedback model
concerns.description: Simulations assume perfect feedback (oracle denotation matches), but live user feedback is noisy; thus simulated annotation-effort reductions and learning curves may be optimistic.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run simulations with realistic, empirically derived noise models (matching observed live error rates and asymmetric error types), and show how performance and annotation fractions change; report robustness to higher noise levels.

concerns.title: Small-scale live deployment limits external validity

evidence: Section 6.2 reports three-stage experiment with 10 new users per stage; authors acknowledge small scale and short duration in shared analysis uncertainty flags.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either expand live deployment (more users, longer time, diverse user demographics) or temper claims; provide additional analysis of query diversity and representativeness to justify external validity.

concerns.title: No analysis of potential model degradation from false-positive user feedback
concerns.description: Even a small fraction of incorrect queries labeled as correct can poison the training set; the paper reports false-positive rate but does not analyze long-term effects or mitigation strategies.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that (a) attention-based seq2seq models can be adapted to emit full SQL, (b) schema-agnostic SQL/templates plus PPDB paraphrases bootstrap domain training without bespoke DB engineering, and (c) an online loop collecting lightweight user feedback plus selective crowd-annotation can rapidly improve a deployed parser while reducing annotation effort. The system uses entity anonymization (TF-IDF span matching) to allow the model to operate on typed placeholders and fills concrete values post-generation. Empirical support is threefold: (1) batch benchmark denotation accuracies on GEO880/ATIS nearly match prior logical-form systems, (2) simulated interactive experiments show faster learning and reduced annotation with templates/paraphrases, and (3) a three-stage small live deployment (academic DB) yields steady improvement and produces the SCHOLAR utterance–SQL dataset. The paper's reasoning chain is: seq2seq with attention + anonymization + schema-derived synthetic templates + paraphrase augmentation => workable initial model for any DB; deploy to users => gather binary/5-way feedback => add user-corrected examples and send incorrect ones to crowd for SQL labels => retrain => improved accuracy and less required annotation over stages. Empirical evaluation supports each link but with limitations in scale, provenance, and some unquantified subcomponents (e.g., TF-IDF linker accuracy, crowd label quality, statistical comparisons to prior works).
logical_argument_graph: Problem: Existing NL-to-DB interfaces require specialized meaning representations or heavy engineering; deploying to new domains is costly.
Core idea: Use attention-based seq2seq models to map NL directly to SQL, avoiding intermediate representations and enabling crowdsourced SQL annotations.

Engineering enablers: (a) Entity anonymization via TF-IDF span matching and typed placeholders; (b) Schema-agnostic language/SQL templates (22) instantiated from schema graph joins; (c) PPDB-based paraphrase augmentation.

Interactive algorithm: Deploy initial model trained on synthetic/templates+paraphrases; collect user feedback (Correct/Incorrect + finer-grained labels); add correct predictions to training; send incorrect examples to crowd workers for SQL annotation; retrain iteratively.
Benchmarks: Evaluate denotation accuracy on GEO880 and ATIS; ablate paraphrasing and templates.
Simulations: Emulate interactive loop with perfect feedback to estimate annotation savings and effect of batch size.
Live experiment: Three-stage deployment on academic database with 30 users; improvement observed and SCHOLAR dataset released.
Conclusion: Combined modeling+augmentation+feedback loop is a practical, incremental approach to bootstrapping NLIDBs with reduced manual engineering and annotation.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that an attention-based seq2seq model can be trained to emit executable SQL directly from natural language and that this enables a practical interactive bootstrapping loop: (1) bootstrap a model using schema-agnostic SQL templates instantiated on the target schema plus PPDB paraphrase expansion, (2) deploy the model to users who mark results with a 5-way feedback interface (treated as binary for learning in most experiments), (3) accept user-marked correct predictions into training, send user-marked incorrect predictions for selective crowd SQL annotation, (4) retrain and iterate. Engineering enablers include entity anonymization via TF-IDF search and filling values post-generation, beam decoding for SQL structure, and using pre-trained embeddings. Empirically the authors: (a) show denotation (execution) accuracy on GEO880 and ATIS roughly comparable to prior systems that target logical forms, (b) report ablations that paraphrasing helps and templates help initial bootstrapping (domain-dependent), (c) present a small live three-stage deployment (30 users) in a scholarly DB (SCHOLAR), showing accuracy rising to ~63.5% and a released 816-example dataset, and (d) simulate interactive learning (perfect feedback) showing annotation savings and batch-size tradeoffs. The conceptual frame advanced is practical, user-driven, data-centric bootstrapping of semantic parsers that privilege executable programs (SQL) and lightweight user signals plus targeted crowd labeling as an operational path to deployable NLIDBs.
logical_argument_graph: N1: Neural seq2seq with attention can generate SQL directly (Section 4.1) -> supports C1.
N2: Entity anonymization (TF-IDF) is needed for generalization and to make SQL generation tractable (Section 4.2) -> enables N1.
N3: Schema-agnostic templates provide initial labeled examples for N1 when no domain data exists (Section 4.3) -> supports rapid bootstrapping.
N4: Paraphrase augmentation (PPDB) increases linguistic coverage of templates and labeled data -> improves generalization (ablation results).
N5: Deploy model online; collect lightweight user feedback (5-way) and treat Correct/Incomplete as positive (Section 6) -> creates signal for additional labeled examples.
N6: Incorrect predictions are selectively sent to crowd workers for SQL annotation -> provides high-quality labeled corrections cheaply.

N7: Iterative retraining on (templates + paraphrases) ∪ user-accepted predictions ∪ crowd-annotated corrections -> improves accuracy and reduces annotation effort over stages (empirical evidence: simulated and live experiments).
N8: Achieved outcomes on benchmarks and a small live deployment (SCHOLAR) demonstrate practical feasibility and release a dataset to catalyze future work (Section 6.3).

identified_claims.claim_text: An attention-based neural sequence-to-sequence model can be trained to directly generate full SQL queries from natural-language utterances, achieving denotation (execution) accuracy on GEO880 and ATIS that is comparable to prior semantic-parsing approaches that target logical forms.
evidence: Section 4.1 describes an encoder-decoder with global attention and beam decoding.
Section 5.3 reports test set denotation accuracies (Table 2/3) and states 'comparable performance' to prior systems.
Shared analysis: 'Our SQL model has slightly lower accuracy than best non-SQL results but is comparable to Dong & Lapata (2016), Jia & Liang (2016)'.

Exact numeric values and statistical tests are referenced in tables but not fully discussed in text; significance unknown.

identified_claims.claim_text: Schema-agnostic synthetic schema templates combined with paraphrase augmentation provide a practical way to bootstrap models for new domains without manual, database-specific engineering.

Section 6.2: first-stage live experiment uses only templates+paraphrases and achieves ~25% correct answers.
Section 6.4 simulated experiments: templates help initial GEO880 stages.

Section 6.2: annotation effort decreased across stages in live run.

Approach may fail on ambiguous or partial references; failure modes not analyzed.

identified_claims.claim_text: The approach is practical: a small online deployment for an academic paper database learned a semantic parser from scratch over three days, produced steady improvement across stages, and yielded a released SCHOLAR dataset of utterance–SQL pairs.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes and evaluates an end-to-end, deployable pipeline that (1) uses an attention-based seq2seq model to map natural-language utterances directly to executable SQL, (2) bootstraps new domains via 22 hand-authored schema-agnostic templates plus PPDB paraphrase augmentation and entity anonymization, and (3) iteratively improves via an online feedback loop where users give lightweight feedback and incorrect predictions are selectively sent to crowd workers for SQL annotation. Evidence includes denotation-based benchmark evaluations (Geo880, ATIS) with ablations, simulated interactive experiments (perfect feedback) exploring batch-size and template/paraphrase effects, and a small live, three-stage deployment on an academic DB producing the SCHOLAR dataset (816 utterance–SQL pairs) with staged accuracy improvements. The overall reasoning chain is coherent: a flexible seq2seq model + anonymization + synthetic seed data yields an initial system; user feedback cheaply identifies correct outputs to add to training and flags incorrect ones for targeted crowd labeling; retraining improves accuracy and reduces annotation load. Key strengths are the integrated engineering, practical focus (SQL output), and mixed evaluation (benchmarks, simulation, small live deployment). Key weaknesses are overstatements or under-quantified links: comparability to prior work (denotation vs logical-form metrics and different splits) is not fully harmonized; entity linking (TF-IDF) lacks quantitative precision/recall and is a critical single point of failure; crowd annotation protocol, quality, and cost are underspecified; paraphrase augmentation noise and template manual effort/generalizability are incompletely measured; live experiment scale is small so external validity is limited. I annotate each main claim with supporting evidence and uncertainty, provide concrete methodological concerns and actionable revision steps, note relevant comparable works, alternative interpretations, and counterfactual conditions under which the contributions would be credible and impactful.
logical_argument_graph: L1: Problem — Existing NLIDB approaches require intermediate representations or extensive feature engineering, making new-domain deployment hard.
L2: Modeling claim — An attention-based encoder-decoder (BiLSTM encoder, global attention, LSTM decoder) can generate full SQL directly from utterances.
L3: Engineering enablers — Entity anonymization (TF-IDF span matching + type placeholders) and post-hoc filling enable generalization across entities.

L4: Bootstrapping claim — Schema-agnostic SQL/language templates (22) + PPDB paraphrase augmentation provide usable synthetic seed data to start learning in a new domain without DB-specific engineering.

L5: Interactive loop claim — Deploying the model and collecting lightweight user feedback (5-way, collapsed to correct/incorrect) and selectively sending incorrect examples to crowd workers for SQL labels creates a train-deploy cycle that improves accuracy and reduces annotation effort.

L6: Empirical checks — Benchmark denotation accuracies (Geo880, ATIS), ablations, simulated interactive runs (perfect feedback), and a small live three-stage deployment (SCHOLAR) support L2–L5 but with noted limitations (metric heterogeneity, small scale, unquantified subcomponents).

L7: Practical outcome — A released SCHOLAR dataset and evidence that the pipeline can learn an initial parser (25% first-stage correct) and reach ~63% in live incremental learning; supervised fully-trained accuracy 67% on SCHOLAR split.

No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals reported; absolute numeric gap to best systems (Jia & Liang etc.) is small but non-zero and sometimes relies on different augmentation techniques.

Simulations assume perfect feedback whereas real user feedback was noisy (false positive/negative rates ~6%), so simulated annotation savings may overestimate real savings.
Crowd annotation quality, cost per annotation, and worker selection are not fully documented; impact on overall cost-effectiveness is unclear.

identified_claims.claim_text: Entity anonymization using a TF-IDF search over database entities and incremental type placeholders permits flexible entity matching in utterances and allows models to generalize across entity mentions and fill concrete values in generated SQL.
evidence: Section 4.2: For spans, query a TF-IDF search engine over DB entities, replace matched span with entity type placeholder (e.g., CITY_NAME_1), and later fill generated SQL using stored mappings.
Qualitative examples: tolerant matching (Donald Knuth vs Donald E. Knuth) mentioned.
uncertainty_flags: There is no quantitative evaluation (precision/recall) of entity linking performance at test time, nor breakdown of failure modes (ambiguous spans, partial names).
Downstream impact on SQL correctness depends on entity linking accuracy; authors note type-highlighting assists users, implying entity-link errors occurred in live runs but not quantified.

identified_claims.claim_text: Using PPDB-based paraphrase augmentation (one-one and one-many large PPDB) consistently improves model performance during training and interactive learning.
evidence: Section 4.3: describes paraphrase expansion (random non-stopword replacement using PPDB) applied to templates and labeled examples.
Section 5.3: ablation mentioned 'paraphrasing using PPDB consistently helps boost performance.'
Section 6.4: simulated experiments show paraphrasing improves performance at all stages.
uncertainty_flags: Quantitative magnitude of improvement from paraphrasing is not fully quoted in main text (referred to ablation tables).
Single-word random paraphrase replacement can introduce semantic shift or ungrammatical utterances; robustness to paraphrase-induced noise is not analyzed.

identified_claims.claim_text: The approach is practical: a small online deployment for an academic paper database yielded steady improvement across three stages and produced a released SCHOLAR dataset of utterance–SQL pairs (816 examples), with a fully supervised parser achieving 67% accuracy on that split.
evidence: Section 6.2: three-stage online experiment with 10 users per stage; final accuracy reported as 63.51%.
Section 6.3: SCHOLAR dataset described (816 utterances), split 600/216; supervised parser accuracy 67%.
Section 7: claims about practicality and release.
uncertainty_flags: Live deployment scale is small and users were likely recruited in a controlled setting; representativeness of user queries is unclear.
SCHOLAR includes crowd-labeled utterances not used in live experiment; provenance and annotation noise are mentioned but not characterized (inter-annotator agreement, worker qualifications, cost).

identified_claims.claim_text: User-provided feedback, using five granular options, has low enough error rates (6.1% false negatives, 6.3% false positives) to allow the interactive learning pipeline to improve models despite noisy signals.
evidence: Section 6.2: Analysis of final-stage user feedback: 6.1% of correctly generated queries marked wrong; 6.3% of incorrect queries marked correct.
Table 6: presents these error rates explicitly.
uncertainty_flags: Error rates are reported only for the final stage (small sample); variability across users, stages, and query types is not reported.
False positives (incorrect predicted SQL marked as correct) are more damaging; the paper reports rate but not downstream impact (e.g., whether mislabeled bad examples degraded later models).

strengths.title: Integrated end-to-end deployable pipeline
strengths.description: The paper combines modeling (seq2seq SQL generation), entity anonymization, synthetic bootstrapping, paraphrase augmentation, user feedback UI, and crowdsourced annotation into a full operational loop.
evidence: Algorithm 1 describes the live train-deploy-retrain loop.
Sections 4.1–4.3 detail modeling, anonymization, and augmentation; Sections 6.1–6.3 show the UI and live deployment.

strengths.title: Practical focus on executable SQL
strengths.description: Targeting SQL enables immediate execution-based evaluation, compatibility with real DBs, and easier crowd annotation by programmers.
evidence: Section 1 and Section 4 motivate parsing directly to SQL.
Section 5 uses denotation (execution) accuracy as the primary metric.

strengths.title: Multiple complementary evaluations
strengths.description: Authors evaluate on standard benchmarks, run ablations and simulated interactive runs, and perform a small live deployment—providing varied empirical evidence.
evidence: Section 5 benchmark experiments with ablations; Section 6 simulated interactive experiments and Section 6.2 live user study.

strengths.title: Released resource (SCHOLAR)
strengths.description: Providing the SCHOLAR utterance–SQL dataset (816 examples) supports reproducibility and further research on academic-domain NLIDBs.
evidence: Section 6.3 describes the dataset and split; Section 7 notes the release.

concerns.title: Comparability to prior work is under-specified
concerns.description: Claims of 'comparable performance' conflate denotation-based accuracy with prior results reported under logical-form exact match or different dataset splits. Without harmonized preprocessing, splits, and statistical testing, the claim risks overstatement.
evidence: Section 5.3 compares denotation accuracies but notes some prior systems use Geo700 vs Geo880 and measure logical form rather than denotation.
Shared analysis notes heterogeneous metrics and pre-processing differences (Geo700/Geo880, logical form vs denotation).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Re-run benchmark comparisons under harmonized conditions: (a) use identical dataset splits and preprocessing as the target comparators, (b) report both denotation and logical-form exact-match where possible (or convert prior outputs), and (c) provide confidence intervals and statistical significance tests for reported differences.

concerns.title: Entity linking (TF-IDF) lacks quantitative evaluation
concerns.description: TF-IDF span matching is a central engineering component; its precision/recall, error modes (ambiguity, partial matches), and downstream effect on SQL correctness are not measured, yet failures can cascade into incorrect SQL and noisy feedback.
evidence: Section 4.2 describes TF-IDF matching qualitatively but provides no quantitative metrics.
Live experiment reports user feedback indicating Wrong Types and execution failures, suggesting entity-linking errors occurred.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report a held-out evaluation of entity linking: precision/recall on annotated entity spans, confusion matrix for types, and an ablation measuring end-to-end SQL accuracy with ground-truth entity linking vs TF-IDF linking.

concerns.title: Crowd annotation protocol and quality/cost unreported
concerns.description: Selective crowd labeling is central to the interactive loop's cost-effectiveness claim but the paper omits details on worker qualifications, annotation interface, inter-annotator agreement, turnaround time, and per-query cost—leaving the operational claim under-supported.
evidence: Sections 3 and 6.2 state that incorrect examples are sent to crowd workers but do not describe annotation protocols or quality metrics.
SCHOLAR dataset includes crowd-labeled examples but provenance/quality control steps are not described.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide documentation on crowd annotation: worker selection criteria, instructions shown to workers, quality control (agreement, verification steps), annotation time/cost per SQL, and an analysis of label noise impact on retrained models.

concerns.title: Paraphrase augmentation noise and effect magnitude underspecified
concerns.description: PPDB-based random single-word paraphrase replacement may introduce semantic drift or ungrammatical sentences; the magnitude and variance of the benefit vs harm are not quantified beyond qualitative ablation mentions.
evidence: Section 4.3 describes the paraphrase method; Section 5.3 reports paraphrasing helps but does not quantify effect sizes in-text.
Shared analysis notes potential semantic shift risk from single-word replacements.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add detailed ablation tables quantifying absolute and relative gains from paraphrasing (with CI) and report error analysis for paraphrase-induced label noise; consider constrained paraphrase strategies (phrase-level, grammar-aware) and report comparative results.

concerns.title: Simulated interactive experiments assume perfect feedback
concerns.description: Simulations use exact-denotation matching as proxy for user feedback, which overestimates performance gains compared to noisy real user feedback (6% error rates reported); thus annotation-effort savings reported may be optimistic.
evidence: Section 6.4 simulation methodology assumes perfect feedback; Section 6.2 reports real user feedback error rates (6.1%/6.3%).
Simulated Table 7 shows annotation percentages that may not hold under noisy feedback.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run simulations that inject realistic noise models (e.g., flip rates matching observed user false positive/negative rates, and asymmetric costs) and report sensitivity of annotation savings and final accuracy to these noise levels.

concerns.title: Template manual effort and generality overclaimed
concerns.description: While templates are labeled 'schema-agnostic', they were manually authored (22 templates). The effort to craft templates and their coverage for multi-entity or complex queries (e.g., ATIS) is not quantified; claiming minimal database-specific engineering needs qualification.
evidence: Section 4.3: 22 hand-written templates described; Section 6.4 notes templates did not help ATIS (complex multi-entity queries).
Shared analysis highlighted that templates are hand-crafted and may not generalize.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report the human time required to author/validate templates, categorize template coverage (which query classes they support), and include experiments showing how additional template classes (e.g., 2-entity templates) change bootstrapping performance.

concerns.title: Limited scale and external validity of live deployment
concerns.description: The live online experiment had only 30 users across three short stages. User population, query diversity, and long-term behavior (e.g., drift, accumulation of noisy labels) are not explored, limiting claims about practical deployability at scale.
evidence: Section 6.2: three stages, 10 new users per stage, 10 utterances minimum each; final accuracy reported for that small cohort.
Shared analysis and other reviewers note small sample and short duration.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either temper claims about broad deployability or run a larger-scale field trial (more users, longer time, varied demographics), and track metrics over time including incidence of noisy accepted incorrect labels and impact on model degradation.

comparable_works.relevance: Directly relevant: neural seq2seq for semantic parsing to logical forms.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar modeling backbone (seq2seq+attention); differs in target representation (logical forms vs SQL) and in reported metrics (logical-form accuracy vs denotation).
comparable_works.source_trace: Retrieved literature; cited in Section 5.3 as comparable neural approach.

comparable_works.relevance: High: neural semantic parsing with data recombination to boost accuracy.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Uses data recombination augmentation; achieved higher accuracy on GEO/ATIS. Their augmentation is compatible and potentially complementary to the paper's approach.

comparable_works.relevance: Relevant: earlier system generating SQL via intermediate representation.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Generates SQL but relies on intermediate representation and SQL-specific engineering; paper contrasts claim of generality without heavy engineering.

comparable_works.relevance: Classic NL2SQL system baseline.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Older rule-based system with strong assumptions; evaluated on Geo700 subset; helps contextualize earlier SQL-oriented approaches.

comparable_works.relevance: Related work on learning from binary correctness signals.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Suggests feasibility of weak feedback signals; differs in target language and learning setup but supports interactive-learning framing.

uncertainty_flags: Metric heterogeneity: comparing denotation accuracy to prior logical-form results without harmonized datasets and preprocessing introduces uncertainty in 'comparable performance' claims.
Entity linking: no precision/recall numbers; TF-IDF may perform poorly on ambiguous/partial mentions.
Crowd annotation: worker selection, QA, cost, and label noise unreported—affects claims about reduced annotation effort and cost-effectiveness.
Paraphrase augmentation: potential semantic drift from single-word replacements is not analyzed quantitatively.
Simulation realism: simulated interactive experiments assume perfect feedback and thus likely overestimate annotation savings.
Live deployment scale: small user sample limits generalizability to real-world, diverse deployments.
alternative_interpretations: The apparent benchmark parity largely reflects compatibility of neural seq2seq methods with denotation-based evaluation, but the model may still underperform on strict logical-form metrics or on complex, multi-entity, long-SQL queries where beam search and grammar constraints matter.

The early-stage performance attributed to templates could be primarily due to paraphrase expansion or pre-trained embeddings rather than the templates themselves; experiments show templates help only for some domains (Geo) but not ATIS.

Reported annotation-effort reductions might be driven mainly by dataset characteristics and simulated-perfect-feedback assumptions; under realistic noisy feedback and noisy crowd labeling, annotation savings could be smaller or require additional QC overhead.

The SCHOLAR dataset's 67% supervised accuracy may reflect mixture of cleaner crowd labels and train/test leakage (e.g., paraphrase overlap), so its generalization potential to new academic corpora is uncertain without further validation.
transparency_notes: The manuscript provides implementation-level details for the model architecture, anonymization pipeline, and augmentation strategies, but omits key operational details about crowd annotation (interface, worker qualifications, QA), and lacks quantitative entity-linking metrics.

Benchmark comparison tables are referenced but do not provide confidence intervals or statistical significance testing; paper acknowledges some prior works use different measures/splits but does not harmonize them.
Simulated interactive experiments are clearly documented as assuming perfect feedback; however, the paper does not present simulations that include measured real-user noise levels.

SCHOLAR dataset construction includes both live-collected utterances and additional crowd-labeled utterances (not used in the live experiment); provenance and quality control steps for the crowd labels are not detailed.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The contribution situates within an active thread (neural program generation, interactive learning), so novelty is incremental and mainly in the integrated, deployable pipeline and use of SQL as the target. Lack of exact analogs is not a sign of invalidity—rather the engineering integration is the contribution; however, empirical claims must be substantiated with robust evaluation.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If TF-IDF entity linking attains high precision/recall (>90%), the anonymization approach will enable accurate value filling and maintain downstream SQL correctness.
If crowd annotations are high quality (verified workers, inter-annotator agreement), then selective annotation of user-flagged failures will rapidly bootstrap the model with low cost.
If templates capture a sufficient fraction of early user intents (or are quickly extended), the initial system will provide helpful results to elicit informative feedback.
If paraphrase augmentation confers robust lexical variability without semantic corruption (controlled PPDB selection), it will consistently improve generalization in low-data stages.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Combines several known components (seq2seq to programs, anonymization, PPDB paraphrases, user feedback loops) into a working end-to-end system targeted at SQL; novelty is in the integrated, operational pipeline rather than a single methodological breakthrough.
evidence: Model components draw on existing literature (Bahdanau et al., Luong et al., Dong & Lapata, PPDB).
Live deployment and SCHOLAR dataset illustrate pragmatic integration.
uncertainty_flags: Degree of engineering novelty depends on details of entity-linking, template instantiation, and feedback workflows which are partially under-specified.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Empirical evidence supports feasibility of direct NL→SQL with seq2seq and of interactive improvement in a small deployment, but claims about parity with prior systems, template generality, and annotation-effort savings need tighter quantification and broader validation.
evidence: Benchmark denotation numbers and staged live accuracy improvements.
Simulated experiments showing annotation fractions under ideal feedback.
uncertainty_flags: Comparability to prior work and external validity of live findings are uncertain due to metric heterogeneity and small-scale live study.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper's core engineering claim (a seq2seq model can generate SQL and be improved via feedback) is well supported by implemented system and experiments, but quantitative claims about parity with prior work, annotation savings, and template generality are uncertain and sensitive to evaluation choices, dataset splits, entity-linking accuracy, crowd quality, and scale. Thus confidence is high that the approach is feasible and practically promising but moderate-to-low for the stronger comparative and generalization claims.

consensus_findings: The manuscript describes a coherent, end-to-end engineering pipeline that maps natural-language utterances to executable SQL using an attention-based seq2seq model, combined with entity anonymization, schema-derived synthetic templates, PPDB paraphrase augmentation, and an interactive user-feedback + selective crowd-annotation loop.

Empirical evidence shows the approach is feasible in practice: the system attains nontrivial denotation (execution) accuracy on GEO880 and ATIS, benefits from paraphrase augmentation in ablations, and can be improved via iterative retraining in both simulated and a small live deployment.

Paraphrase augmentation (PPDB) and schema templates play meaningful roles in low-data bootstrapping, though their effectiveness is domain-dependent (helpful for some datasets/domains, less so for others).

Entity anonymization (TF-IDF span matching + typed placeholders) is a central engineering mechanism for generalization and value re-insertion, but its behavior is reported qualitatively rather than quantitatively.
The live interactive experiment and SCHOLAR dataset are valuable operational artifacts demonstrating a proof-of-concept deployment, but the live trial is small in scale and duration.
disagreements: Degree of empirical parity with prior work: reviewers agree that denotation-level performance is promising, but disagree about how strong the 'comparable to prior semantic-parsing systems' claim is because prior work uses heterogeneous metrics (logical-form vs denotation) and sometimes different splits — some reviewers treat reported parity as plausible, others view it as under-specified and needing harmonized re-runs.

Strength of the 'no manual engineering' claim for bootstrapping via templates: some reviewers see the 22 hand-authored schema-agnostic templates as modest, practical manual effort consistent with the claim's spirit; others treat the templates themselves as manual engineering that should be acknowledged and quantified.

Severity of paraphrase-noise risk: reviewers uniformly note paraphrasing helps in ablation, but they differ on how concerning random single-word PPDB substitutions are absent a detailed noise analysis (some rate this as a moderate risk requiring experiments, others consider it a smaller practical issue).

Interpretation of interactive-loop gains: reviewers accept that iterative retraining improves accuracy, but differ on whether gains come mainly from user-accepted examples, crowd-annotated corrections, template/paraphrase augmentation, or dataset characteristics — i.e., the causal attribution among components is disputed.
uncertainty_hotspots: Benchmark comparability: whether denotation-based numbers reported are truly comparable to prior logical-form baselines given differing metrics, preprocessing, and dataset splits (Geo700 vs Geo880).

Entity linking (TF-IDF) performance: precision/recall, common failure modes (ambiguous/partial names, paraphrases), and the quantitative downstream effect of linking errors on SQL execution and feedback quality remain unmeasured.

Crowd annotation pipeline: worker qualification, inter-annotator agreement, annotation latency, per-example cost, and label noise are not reported but are critical to the cost-effectiveness claim of selective annotation.

Realism of simulated interactive experiments: simulations assume perfect/oracle feedback; real user feedback is noisy (reported ~6% false positives/negatives) and asymmetric harms (false positives more damaging) are not modeled in simulations.

Template coverage and manual effort: how representative the 22 templates are for other schemas, the human time required to author them, and whether more complex multi-entity query patterns require extra templates are unclear.

Long-term dynamics of noisy user feedback: potential for harmful accumulation of false-positive 'correct' markings and whether safeguards are needed to prevent model drift are not empirically addressed.
model_diversity_effects: Structure-analyst perspective emphasized logical coherence and chaining of components, highlighting under-specified links (entity linking -> feedback -> retraining) and calling for componentwise ablations and provenance tracking.

Methodology-auditor perspective prioritized reproducibility and measurement: requests harmonized baselines, statistical tests, random seeds, and explicit preprocessing; flagged missing crowdsourcing details and entity-link metrics as methodological gaps.

Novelty-assessor (incremental) judged the work a useful engineering integration with moderate novelty; novelty-assessor (disruptive) framed the SQL-target + feedback-loop as a practical reframing with potential impact but contingent on empirical robustness.

Claim-verifier stressed evidence-first concerns and required concrete empirical quantification (precision/recall, cost, error-attribution) before accepting operational claims about annotation-effort reductions at scale.

These role-specific emphases produced diverse priorities for revisions (e.g., editor should demand reproducibility artifacts; authors should add targeted experiments on entity linking and crowd annotation), but reviewers agree on core empirical gaps to address.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Use the editor role to coordinate targeted revisions rather than a binary decision. Requested revisions should focus on improving reproducibility and resolving the principal empirical uncertainties before stronger generalization claims are circulated. Specifically, ask authors to: (1) harmonize benchmark comparisons: re-run or clearly map baselines under identical preprocessing/splits and report denotation vs logical-form metrics with confidence intervals and random-seed details; (2) quantify entity-linking behavior with held-out precision/recall/F1, and include an ablation showing performance with oracle vs TF-IDF linking; (3) fully describe the crowd annotation protocol (worker qualification, instructions, quality-control measures, inter-annotator agreement, latency and cost per SQL), and provide an analysis of crowd label noise; (4) extend simulations and/or rerun interactive experiments injecting empirically measured feedback noise (including asymmetric false-positive rates) to show sensitivity of annotation savings and long-term model behavior; (5) provide explicit documentation of the 22 templates (examples), the human effort required to create them, and an analysis of their coverage; (6) surface full numeric tables, random seeds, hyperparameters, preprocessing code, and data splits (release scripts) to enable reproducibility. Prioritize experiments (1)-(4) above; if full re-deployment is infeasible, require realistic simulations and ablations that use the live-measured noise profiles. Keep editorial communication central: request that authors summarize which claims will be qualified in revised text versus which additional results will be provided to substantiate stronger claims.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript, provide focused evidence and clarifications addressing the reviewers' main uncertainties: (A) Benchmarks: report exact preprocessing scripts, random seeds, and dataset splits; re-evaluate or clarify which prior numbers are not directly comparable; add bootstraped confidence intervals and, if feasible, re-run one or two key baselines under your preprocessing. (B) Entity linking: create a small annotated test set of entity mentions (from SCHOLAR or benchmarks) and report TF-IDF precision/recall/F1; run an ablation with oracle entity linking to quantify its contribution to end-to-end denotation accuracy and error types. (C) Crowdsourcing: document worker qualifications, annotation instructions, verification/QA steps, inter-annotator agreement, per-example time and monetary cost, and an analysis of label noise; indicate how crowd labels were used when building SCHOLAR (provenance). (D) Interactive-loop realism: run simulations that inject realistic noise matching live user error rates (asymmetric false-positive/false-negative), and report sensitivity of annotation fractions and final accuracy to those noise levels; if possible, re-analyze live-run data to attribute gains to user-accepted vs crowd-annotated examples. (E) Templates & paraphrases: publish the 22 templates, report human effort (hours) to author them, and include experiments showing how additional template classes or constrained paraphrase selection affect cold-start performance. (F) Transparency: release preprocessing code, anonymization scripts, PPDB subset parameters, and full numeric tables to enable replication. Explicitly qualify claims in the text where evidence is domain-limited (small live pilot) or dependent on unquantified components.
transparency_report: Missing or insufficiently-detailed items needed for reproducibility and assessment: (a) exact preprocessing pipeline and dataset splits for GEO880/ATIS (scripts, tokenization, anonymization steps), (b) random seeds and training-run variance / confidence intervals for reported accuracies, (c) full numeric benchmark tables (including baselines) with clear denotation vs logical-form labeling, (d) entity-linking code and a held-out evaluation (precision/recall) for TF-IDF matching and example failure cases, (e) exact PPDB subsets used, paraphrase sampling strategy details and seeds, and paraphrase filter thresholds (if any), (f) the 22 schema templates and documentation of the human effort to author them, (g) crowd annotation protocol: worker qualifications, instructions, interface screenshots, verification/QC, inter-annotator agreement statistics, per-example latency and cost, (h) provenance of SCHOLAR examples (which came from live users vs crowd labeling), and (i) logs or breakdowns showing which retraining examples originated from user 'accepts' versus crowd corrections.

Authors are encouraged to publish code, preprocessing scripts, anonymization/index-building code, template specification, and a single reproducible training run (seeded) that yields reported numbers or a small range around them.
epistemic_limits: The synthesis is constrained by the content and experiments reported in the manuscript and the reviewers' independent readings; it does not include access to the authors' unreleased code, raw annotation logs, or the full numeric tables unless provided. Key unresolved empirical questions (entity-link accuracy, crowd label quality/cost, harmonized baselines) prevent definitive claims about generalization, cost-efficiency, and parity with prior methods. The live deployment evidence is a small-scale proof-of-concept; scaling behavior, long-term label-poisoning dynamics, and applicability to more complex/heterogeneous schemas remain empirically open. Where reviewers diverge (e.g., on strength of novelty or practical impact), this reflects different role-driven priors (methodological rigor vs engineering utility) rather than contradictions in the underlying reported facts. Accordingly, the editor should treat claims that depend on unreported quantities (e.g., 'no manual engineering' or 'comparable to prior work') as contingent and request the targeted experiments and documentation outlined above before stronger generalization statements are accepted.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript describes an end-to-end engineering pipeline that trains an attention-based sequence-to-sequence model to emit executable SQL from natural-language utterances, bootstraps new domains using 22 hand-authored schema-agnostic SQL/language templates plus PPDB paraphrase augmentation, anonymizes entities via a TF-IDF lookup-and-placeholder approach, and iteratively improves via a deployed interactive loop combining lightweight user feedback and selective crowd annotation. Empirical evidence includes denotation-based results on GEO880 and ATIS (reported as comparable to prior semantic-parsing work), ablation results showing paraphrase benefits, simulated interactive experiments (assuming oracle feedback) analyzing batch/annotation tradeoffs, and a small three-stage live deployment producing the SCHOLAR dataset (816 utterance–SQL pairs) with staged accuracy gains.
strengths: Presents a coherent, implemented end-to-end pipeline from model architecture through anonymization, synthetic seeding, UI for user feedback, selective crowd annotation, and iterative retraining — culminating in a small live deployment and a released dataset (SCHOLAR).

Practical engineering choices (targeting executable SQL, anonymization to reduce sparsity, and selective crowd labeling of failures) make crowd annotation feasible and align with deployment considerations.

Provides multiple complementary evaluations: benchmark denotation experiments (GEO880, ATIS), ablations (paraphrasing and template use), simulated interactive analyses, and a live multi-stage pilot with logged user feedback statistics.
limitations: Benchmark comparability and statistical reporting: key claims of being 'comparable to prior semantic-parsing systems' mix denotation-based evaluation and prior logical-form metrics, and baselines/splits (Geo700 vs Geo880) are heterogeneous. The manuscript lacks harmonized re-runs, variance estimates (confidence intervals or standard errors), and explicit mapping of which prior numbers are denotation vs logical-form, undermining the strength of the comparative claim.

Unquantified entity-linking performance: the TF-IDF-based anonymization is central to end-to-end correctness, yet no quantitative precision/recall/F1 or failure-mode analysis is reported. Without an oracle-vs-real linking ablation, the contribution of entity resolution to final SQL accuracy and the sensitivity of the pipeline to linking errors remain unclear.

Under-specified crowd annotation pipeline and costs: selective crowd labeling is critical to the interactive loop's cost-effectiveness, but worker qualification, interface/instruction design, inter-annotator agreement, annotation latency, per-example monetary cost, and observed label noise are not documented, making operational scaling claims hard to evaluate.

Limited scale and realism of interactive evaluation: the live deployment is small (three stages, ~30 users total) and simulated interactive experiments assume perfect/oracle feedback. Real user feedback was noisy (~6% false positives/negatives reported in one stage), and the long-term dynamics of noisy accepted incorrect labels (potential model poisoning) are not simulated or measured.
open_questions: Please provide a harmonized benchmark comparison: can authors re-run principal baselines or report their model under the exact preprocessing/splits used by the cited prior works (or vice versa), and provide confidence intervals / standard errors for reported denotation accuracies? Which prior numbers are not directly comparable (denotation vs logical form) and how does this affect interpretation?

Can authors release a held-out annotated set of entity mentions and report TF-IDF entity-linking precision/recall/F1 at test time, plus an ablation comparing end-to-end denotation accuracy with oracle (perfect) entity linking vs TF-IDF linking to quantify impact?

Please document the crowd annotation process used for selective correction and for SCHOLAR: worker qualification filters, the annotation instructions or UI, inter-annotator agreement statistics, average annotation time and monetary cost per SQL, and procedures for quality control or dispute resolution.

How sensitive are simulated annotation-savings and learning curves to realistic, empirically measured user-feedback noise? Please run simulations that inject asymmetric false-positive/false-negative rates matching live observations and report whether annotation fractions and final accuracies degrade materially; and, empirically, can the authors disaggregate gains attributable to user-accepted vs crowd-annotated examples in the live run?
consensus_snapshot: All reviewers agree the paper contributes a useful, coherent engineering pipeline that makes direct NL→SQL via seq2seq feasible and operationally interesting, and that the live pilot and SCHOLAR dataset are valuable proof-of-concept artifacts.

All reviewers note paraphrase augmentation and schema templates materially aid cold-start performance in some domains and that anonymization plus value re-insertion is an important enabling engineering trick.

All reviewers request stronger quantitative analysis of unmeasured components (entity linking, crowd annotation, and benchmark comparability) and more realistic simulations of noisy feedback before broader generalization claims are made.
disagreement_snapshot: Some reviewers view the 22 schema-agnostic templates as modest, practical manual effort consistent with the manuscript's spirit; others consider the templates themselves to be manual engineering that should be acknowledged and measured (time and coverage).

Reviewers differ on how severely to treat paraphrase-noise risk: several see it as a moderate issue needing empirical analysis; a minority view it as a lower-priority implementation detail since ablations show net benefit in reported datasets.

There is divergence on the strength of the 'comparable to prior work' claim: some reviewers treat the denotation-level parity as plausible and promising; others demand harmonized baselines and statistical tests before accepting that parity.
uncertainty_snapshot: Uncertainty about generalization to other schemas and larger, noisier user populations due to small scale of live deployment and lack of long-term iterative data.

Uncertainty about the magnitude and direction of error propagation through the pipeline (entity-linking errors -> wrong SQL execution -> noisy user feedback -> potential harmful training examples), because entity-link and crowd-label statistics are not reported.
Uncertainty in the extent to which annotation-effort reductions observed in oracle simulations hold under measured user feedback noise and realistic crowd annotation error rates and costs.
source_trace: Dong, L. & Lapata, M. (2016). 'Language to Logical Form with Neural Attention' — referenced as closest neural baseline (paper Section 5.3 comparisons); reviewers flagged metric differences (logical form vs denotation) as a comparability issue.

Jia, R. & Liang, P. (2016). 'Data Recombination for Neural Semantic Parsing' — cited by authors as complementary augmentation work; reviewers recommend comparing/reproducing under identical preprocessing.
PPDB (Ganitkevitch et al., 2013) — the paraphrase resource used for augmentation (Section 4.3); reviewers request statistics on paraphrase sampling and noise.

Poon (2013) / Popescu et al. (2003) — prior SQL-oriented systems referenced in related work (Section 2, 5.3); reviewers use these to contextualize claims about manual engineering and SQL-targeting approaches.

transparency_notes: Key reproducibility and transparency gaps identified that should be remedied: (1) publish preprocessing scripts, tokenization and anonymization code, and exact dataset splits (GEO/ATIS processed versions) and random seeds used for runs; (2) supply full numeric benchmark tables including baselines and indicate for each whether numbers are denotation or logical-form metrics; (3) release the 22 schema templates and document the human time/effort to author them; (4) publish TF-IDF entity-index construction code and an annotated held-out entity mention set with reported precision/recall/F1; (5) provide full documentation of the crowd annotation protocol used (instructions, qualification filters, inter-annotator agreement, per-example time and cost) and provenance labeling for SCHOLAR examples (which were live-collected vs crowd-annotated); (6) detail PPDB subset choices and paraphrase sampling seeds and thresholds; (7) when reporting interactive/simulation results, include runs that inject empirically measured user-feedback noise and asymmetric flip rates.

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The paper presents a practical, end-to-end system that maps natural language to executable SQL using an attention-based seq2seq model, bootstraps cold-start performance using 22 schema-agnostic templates plus PPDB paraphrases, handles values via TF-IDF-based anonymization, and iteratively improves through a deployed interactive loop combining lightweight user feedback and selective crowd annotation. Empirical evidence spans denotation-based benchmarks (GEO880, ATIS), ablations showing paraphrase benefits, simulated interactive experiments, and a small three-stage live deployment that produced the SCHOLAR dataset.

Strengths:
- A complete, implemented pipeline from modeling through deployment and dataset release; useful as an applied systems contribution.
- Practical emphasis on SQL as the target language makes crowd labeling feasible and enables denotation-based evaluation.
- Multiple evaluation modalities (benchmarks, ablations, simulation, live pilot) provide converging evidence of feasibility.

Limitations:
- Benchmark comparability: reported denotation accuracies are not harmonized against prior works that report logical-form metrics or use different splits; no confidence intervals/statistical tests are provided. This undercuts the strength of parity claims.
- Entity-linking is unmeasured quantitatively: TF-IDF matching is described but lacks precision/recall/F1 or oracle ablation, leaving a critical single point of failure unquantified.
- Crowd annotation pipeline and costs are under-documented: worker qualifications, agreement, interface, per-example time and monetary cost, and label noise handling are missing, which are necessary to assess operational cost-effectiveness.
- Limited scale/realism of interactive evaluation: the live deployment is small (30 users) and simulated interactive experiments assume perfect feedback; real feedback is noisy (~6% error rates reported) and long-term accumulation of false-positive accepted labels is unexamined.

Open Questions:
1) Please provide harmonized benchmark runs (or clearly explain mapping) and report variance estimates—how do denotation numbers compare under identical preprocessing and splits to key baselines (Dong & Lapata 2016, Jia & Liang 2016)?
2) Can the authors release or report an annotated entity-mention test set and TF-IDF linking precision/recall, and include an ablation with oracle linking to show its contribution to final SQL correctness?
3) Provide full documentation of the crowd annotation workflow used for selective corrections and SCHOLAR creation: worker screening, instructions, agreement, turnaround time, and per-item cost—how noisy were crowd labels and how were errors handled?
4) Re-run simulations (or retrain) injecting realistic asymmetric feedback noise matching observed live error rates; how sensitive are annotation-savings and final accuracy to increasing false-positive rates? Also, in the live run, what fraction of final-stage gains are attributable to user-accepted examples vs crowd-annotated corrections?

Transparency:
The manuscript should release preprocessing code, anonymization/index-building scripts, the 22 schema templates, PPDB subset/selection details, random seeds, full numeric tables (including baselines and denotation vs logical-form labels), and the crowd-annotation protocol and SCHOLAR provenance. These items are necessary to reproduce reported results and to evaluate operational claims about annotation savings and deployment feasibility.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects high certainty about identified engineering contributions and observed small-scale empirical findings (benchmarks, live pilot) but moderate uncertainty about broader claims because of unreported components (entity-linking metrics, crowd-label quality/cost, harmonized baseline comparisons) and small-scale interactive evaluation. The interval encodes strong evidence for feasibility but substantial uncertainty about generalization and robustness.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
